UNIT 4 — MEIOSIS (Reduction Division)
What Is It?

Meiosis is the special type of cell division that makes sperm and egg cells (gametes). One parent cell (2n = 46) divides TWICE to make four haploid daughter cells (n = 23). It's called 'reduction division' because the chromosome number is halved — this is essential so that when sperm + egg fuse, the zygote gets back to 46.
The Two Divisions
Meiosis I (Reduction Division) — 5 stages:
Prophase I — Homologous chromosomes PAIR UP (synapsis) and exchange DNA (crossing over). This is where genetic variation is created. Mnemonic: 'P1 = PAIR UP'.
Metaphase I — Homologous PAIRS line up in the middle (not individual chromosomes like mitosis). Mnemonic: 'M1 = pairs in the MIDDLE'.
Anaphase I — The PAIRS separate — one of each pair goes to each pole. Sister chromatids stay together. Mnemonic: 'A1 = Apart, but still in pairs'.
Telophase I — Two cells form, each with n = 23 chromosomes (but each chromosome still has 2 chromatids).
Cytokinesis I — Cell splits into two haploid cells.
Meiosis II (Equational Division) — almost identical to mitosis:
Prophase II — Chromosomes condense again; spindle reforms.
Metaphase II — Individual chromosomes line up in the middle (not pairs).
Anaphase II — Sister chromatids separate (just like mitosis anaphase).
Telophase II — Four haploid cells form; nuclear membranes rebuild.
Cytokinesis II — Final split → 4 single-chromatid gametes (n = 23).
Why It Matters
Sexual reproduction — without meiosis, chromosome number would double every generation.
Genetic variation — crossing over in Prophase I shuffles genes, so no two gametes (and no two siblings) are identical.
Independent assortment — which homologous pair goes to which pole is random, adding more variation.
Mnemonic
'M1 = Pairs Apart, M2 = chromatids Apart'
Meiosis I separates PAIRS (homologous chromosomes). Meiosis II separates chromatids (just like mitosis).
Memory: 'I = one pair, II = two chromatids apart'
Key Difference: Mitosis vs Meiosis (for this unit)
Mitosis: 1 division → 2 identical diploid cells (body cells).
Meiosis: 2 divisions → 4 different haploid cells (gametes).
Crossing over happens ONLY in meiosis (Prophase I) — not in mitosis.
Quick Test
Q1. How many divisions does meiosis have? → Two (Meiosis I and Meiosis II).
Q2. How many daughter cells does one meiosis produce? → Four, each haploid (n = 23 in humans).
Q3. When does crossing over happen? → Prophase I (homologous chromosomes exchange segments).
Q4. What is independent assortment? → The random orientation of homologous pairs in Metaphase I.
Q5. Why is meiosis essential for sexual reproduction? → It halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores 2n.
